title: The Human Body
description: Ten calm, clear essays and stories about the human body: the heart's valves, the immune system as a city's defense, the inner ear and balance, how bones heal, the liver's many jobs, the science of a yawn, how the eye adjusts to the dark, the gut's bacteria, wrinkled fingers in the pool and a town's fight for clean water.

lessons.title: Four Doors in the Heart
lessons.summary: An essay on how the heart's four valves keep blood moving in one direction.
lessons.text:
It is common to call the heart a pump. The description is not inaccurate, but it is incomplete, and an incomplete picture can be as misleading as an inaccurate one. A pump that only pushed would achieve little if the blood could flow straight back. The heart moves blood in one direction only, and that achievement belongs to four small valves, the doors through which every drop must pass.

The heart sits in the chest clad in a thin, tough sac. Inside, it has four chambers: two smaller ones above and two larger, stronger ones below. The upper chambers work like a funnel: they gather the blood that returns from the body and the lungs and funnel it downward. A valve separates each upper chamber from the one below it, and two more valves guard the exits.

None of these valves has a muscle of its own. They are thin flaps of tissue, clad in the same smooth lining that covers the inside of the blood vessels, and they open and close for one reason only: pressure. When the pressure behind a valve is greater than the pressure in front of it, the flaps are pushed open. When the pressure reverses, the blood itself presses them shut. In the valves between the chambers, fine cords hold the flaps like the ropes of a sail, so that they close evenly and are never blown backward. The exit valves have three small cups instead, which fill with blood whenever it tries to flow back, swell, and meet evenly in the middle.

The familiar double sound of a heartbeat is the sound of these doors closing: first the two valves between the chambers, then, a moment later, the two exit valves.

The figures involved are formidable. A resting heart beats about 70 times a minute, roughly 100,000 times a day and well over 2 billion times in a long life. If we measured a heart's mileage the way we measure a car's, no engine built by human hands could match it, and a car with that mileage would have been retired long ago. The heart's reliability is perhaps even more formidable than its strength.

That work begins remarkably early. From its inception, the heart is among the first organs to function: it starts to beat about three weeks after conception, before its valves have fully formed. From that inception until the last day of life, it never stops to rest.

Seen narrowly, the valves are simple flaps that respond to pressure. Seen less narrowly, they are a hugely elegant solution to a hard problem: how to keep a liquid moving forward, without thought or effort, for a hundred years. They are tiny, but their task is hugely important.

Questions:
Why is it incomplete to call the heart a pump?
Because a pump that only pushed would achieve little if the blood could flow back; the valves make the blood move in one direction only.
What makes the valves open and close?
Pressure opens and closes them, since none of the valves has a muscle of its own.
How do the exit valves close evenly?
Their three small cups fill with blood, swell and meet evenly in the middle.
Why does the text compare the heart's mileage with a car's?
Because the heart beats more than 2 billion times in a long life, and no engine built by human hands could match that mileage.

lessons.title: The City Within
lessons.summary: The immune system pictured as the defense of an old walled city.
lessons.text:
Imagine the body as an old walled city, and the immune system as everything the city does to protect itself. The skin is its wall, and the moist surfaces of the nose, the throat and the gut are covered with sticky fluids that trap visitors before they can climb over. Like barbed wire on top of a fence, these barriers do not choose their targets. Barbed wire stops a friend and a stranger alike; it simply makes entry difficult for everyone.

Some visitors get through anyway. Inside the walls, they meet the city's night watch: cells that patrol the streets and attack anything that looks foreign. These guards are fast and ruthless. They do not stop to ask questions; they surround suspicious bacteria and swallow them whole. Their weapons are blunt, more like a club than a dagger.

When the night watch cannot finish the job, it raises the alarm, and the city begins to muster its army. Messengers carry pieces of the enemy to small glands throughout the body, where the city's specialists convene.

Here the defense becomes precise. The body holds millions of specialist cells, and each recognizes one particular shape. When a messenger arrives with a piece of the perpetrator, the specialists who convene there are tested, and the few whose receptors fit it best are chosen. The strength of that fit is called affinity. The cells with the highest affinity multiply, and over several days they muster into a large force. Some produce antibodies, which mark the perpetrator for destruction. Others work like a dagger, finding infected cells and destroying them one at a time. As the battle goes on, the affinity of the antibodies improves, like the aim of an archer.

Not every perpetrator is easy to catch. Some viruses evade detection by changing their outer coats; this is one reason a new flu vaccine is prepared each year. Others hide inside the body's own cells. In the old Greek story, the Trojans pulled a wooden horse inside the walls of Troy, unaware that it was full of soldiers. A hiding virus plays the part of the horse, and the body plays the part of the Trojans. Yet an infected cell displays pieces of what is inside it on its surface, like a flag in a window, so the virus cannot evade inspection for long.

After the battle, a few specialists remain as memory cells, ready to muster an army quickly if the same enemy returns. This memory is the principle behind vaccination.

A ruthless defense has a cost. When the guards mistake a harmless visitor for an enemy, the result is an allergy. Most of the time, however, the city keeps its balance: ruthless toward enemies, gentle toward its own citizens.

Questions:
How are the skin and the body's sticky fluids like barbed wire?
They do not choose their targets; they simply make entry difficult for everyone.
What is affinity?
Affinity is the strength of the fit between a specialist cell and the shape of the perpetrator.
How do some viruses evade detection?
They change their outer coats, so that the specialists no longer recognize them.
How does the text compare a hiding virus to the Trojan horse?
The virus plays the part of the horse, and the body plays the part of the Trojans who pulled it inside the walls.

lessons.title: The Level in Your Ear
lessons.summary: How the inner ear senses turning and tilting, and how the brain uses it to keep us balanced.
lessons.text:
Close your eyes and tilt your head. You know at once which way you have moved. That knowledge comes from a small organ deep inside the ear.

The inner ear contains three tiny curved tubes, filled with fluid and set at right angles to one another. When the head turns, the fluid lags slightly behind, like coffee in a cup when you turn the cup. This bends fine hairs inside the tubes, and the hairs send signals to the brain. Because each tube points in a different direction, the brain can detect any kind of turning.

Next to the tubes lie two small chambers that sense gravity and movement in a straight line, such as the lift of an elevator. Their hairs are covered by a layer of jelly topped with tiny crystals, heavier than the fluid around them. The crystals behave rather like sediment at the bottom of a pond: when the head tilts, the sediment slides a little, pulling on the hairs below. Our distant aquatic ancestors already had something similar, and many aquatic animals today use the same principle.

The brain is the nexus where all these signals meet. Information from the ear, the eyes and the muscles arrives here, and at this nexus the brain builds a single sense of where the body is. One result is a remarkable reflex. Shake your head gently while reading this sentence, and the words stay clear. The reflex moves the eyes in the opposite direction almost instantly, keeping the image still.

When the signals disagree, the brain struggles. On a ship, the ear feels the floor rising and falling while the eyes, fixed on the walls of a cabin, report no motion; the messages scramble, and the traveler feels sick. Pilots in thick clouds face a similar problem: without a horizon, the ear's sense of tilt can be skewed, so pilots learn to trust their instruments over their feelings.

People who jump with a parachute often say that after the first few seconds the feeling of falling disappears: once the push of the air balances the pull of gravity, the body stops speeding up, and the crystals sense nothing unusual. Only when the parachute opens does the ear notice a change.

A blow to the head can also skew or scramble these signals for a while. After a concussion, balance may feel slightly wrong, and balance tests are a common part of examining a concussion.

Balance also changes drastically over a lifetime. The brain needs years of practice to use the organ well. That is why a toddler's first steps are lumbering and uncertain, like the walk of a bear, and why, a few years later, the same child can run, spin and ride a bicycle. Few skills improve so drastically in so short a time.

Questions:
Why does the text compare the crystals to sediment?
Because, like sediment in a pond, they slide a little when the head tilts.
Why do pilots learn to trust their instruments?
Because without a horizon, the ear's sense of tilt can be skewed.
Why does the feeling of falling disappear during a parachute jump?
Once the push of the air balances the pull of gravity, the body stops speeding up, and the crystals sense nothing unusual.
How does balance change drastically in childhood?
A toddler walks with lumbering steps, but a few years later the same child can run and ride a bicycle.

lessons.title: How a Bone Mends
lessons.summary: How a broken bone heals, and what healed bones tell scholars about the past.
lessons.text:
Bone looks like the most permanent material in the body, hard and dry like stone. In fact it is living tissue, furnished with blood vessels and nerves and constantly renewed.

When a bone breaks, blood gathers around the broken ends and soon forms a soft mass that seals the area. Over the following days, the body lays down a soft bridge of tough fibers across the gap. After about a fortnight, that is, two weeks, the bridge begins to harden as minerals, mostly calcium, are deposited in it. In the weeks that follow, it becomes a rough collar of new bone, thicker than the original, which holds the broken ends firmly together.

The bone is now joined, but it is not finished. The final stage can last for months or even years. Two kinds of cells take part. One kind works like a demolition crew: it dissolves old or unnecessary bone. The other follows like a team of builders, furnished with fresh minerals, and lays down new bone. Together, demolition and construction slowly shape the rough collar until the bone returns close to its original form.

This partnership goes on throughout life and responds to the loads the bones carry. Astronauts who spend months in space, where the body has no weight to carry, lose bone, because the demolition crews keep working while the builders slow down. No bone stays strong indefinitely without use; a bone that is used, however, can renew itself almost indefinitely.

Because bone keeps a record of its injuries, it is one of the richest sources of information about the past, and anthropology, the study of human beings and their cultures, relies on it heavily. A scholar of anthropology examining a skeleton from antiquity can often tell whether a broken bone healed, and how well. A healed leg tells a quiet story: someone must have fed and protected the injured person for many weeks. Evidence of this kind has led some scholars to rethink old ideas about early communities, once imagined as harsh places where the weak were left behind. They are also rethinking how much care people in antiquity were able to give.

Bones also record hard times. A period of famine in childhood can leave thin lines across the long bones, where growth stopped for a while and then resumed. Modern scanners can find old fractures or signs of famine in an Egyptian mummy without opening it. The skeleton of a samurai, a warrior of old Japan, might show a healed arm. Whether the bones belonged to a samurai, a farmer in Peru or a mummy in Egypt, the same patient record is written in them.

Questions:
What happens to the soft bridge after about a fortnight?
It begins to harden as minerals, mostly calcium, are deposited in it.
What do the two kinds of cells do in the final stage?
One kind works like a demolition crew and dissolves old bone, and the other lays down new bone like a team of builders.
What can a healed leg from antiquity tell a scholar of anthropology?
It tells that someone must have fed and protected the injured person for many weeks.
How can a period of famine be seen in the bones?
It can leave thin lines across the long bones, where growth stopped for a while and then resumed.

lessons.title: The Body's Refinery
lessons.summary: An essay on the liver: how it stores and rations fuel, cleans the blood, warms the body and regrows.
lessons.text:
If the heart is the body's pump, the liver is its refinery. An oil refinery takes crude oil and turns it into fuel, plastics and countless other products; the liver takes the raw materials delivered by the gut and turns them into what the body needs. It is the largest organ inside the body, and it performs hundreds of tasks.

Almost everything we eat passes through this refinery before it reaches the rest of the body. Blood from the gut flows through a large vein straight to the liver. Suppose you eat a sweet pastry and a ripe mango for breakfast. The sugar from the pastry and the mango reaches the blood quickly, and the liver removes much of it and stores it in a compact form.

It is tempting to equate the liver with a simple warehouse, but it is closer to a careful manager. Between meals and through the night, it releases the stored sugar a little at a time, rationing its supplies so that the brain, which depends on a steady flow, never runs short. People sometimes crave something sweet in the late afternoon and imagine that their body has run out of fuel. Usually the liver has been feeding the brain all along, and the wish for a tempting snack has more to do with habit than with need.

The liver can ration only what it has stored, and it can store only so much. When we binge on sweets, eating far more than the body can use, the liver cannot keep all the extra sugar, so it turns the excess into fat. The organ was designed for steady meals rather than feasts, and every binge tests its limits.

The liver also breaks down old blood cells, medicines and many substances the body does not need. It makes bile, a fluid that helps the gut digest fat. It stores vitamins and iron. We tend to equate importance with size or noise, but this quiet organ is among the busiest in the body.

Its work never stops. A factory can plan a shutdown for repairs, but the liver must keep running every hour of every day; a complete shutdown is not an option. Its answer to damage is remarkable: if part of a healthy liver is removed, the rest can grow back to nearly its original size within a few months.

The liver is also a kind of burner. Its chemical work releases a great deal of heat, and at rest it helps to keep the whole body warm, like a burner that never goes out. Most of us, however, keep the liver on the back burner of our attention, an expression borrowed from cooking for something we rarely think about. We crave the pastry; we never think of the organ that will deal with it.

Questions:
Why does the text call the liver a refinery?
Because it takes the raw materials delivered by the gut and turns them into what the body needs, as an oil refinery turns crude oil into fuel.
How does the liver ration its supplies?
Between meals and through the night, it releases the stored sugar a little at a time, so that the brain never runs short.
What happens when we binge on sweets?
The liver cannot keep all the extra sugar, so it turns the excess into fat.
What does the expression "on the back burner" mean?
It means something we rarely think about.

lessons.title: Why We Yawn
lessons.summary: A columnist explores what science knows about yawning and why yawns spread.
lessons.text:
I should confess that, before I became a columnist, I was a hater of meetings. For six years I worked at a telecom company, where we met every morning to discuss figures that nobody remembered by lunch. I still cringe when I remember the morning my manager stopped in the middle of a sentence, looked straight at me and asked whether he was keeping me awake. I had yawned in front of everyone.

So when a reader wrote to ask why we yawn, I decided it was time to ponder the question properly.

A yawn is a reflex, not a choice. It lasts about six seconds: a long, deep breath with the mouth wide open, a stretch of the jaw, then a shorter breath out. Babies do it even before they are born, and so do fish and birds.

For a long time, the popular explanation was that we yawn to take in more oxygen. It is a neat idea, but experiments have not supported it: people given extra oxygen to breathe yawn just as often. A newer theory proposes that it helps to cool the brain; another, that it helps us move from sleep to waking or from rest to attention. Scientists still ponder which is right.

The strangest feature of a yawn is that it spreads. Seeing someone do it, or even reading about it, can set off your own. Researchers have found that this spreading follows the lines of intimacy. We are more likely to catch a yawn from a family member or a close friend than from a stranger, as if intimacy left us more open to one another's moods.

Dogs sometimes catch it from their owners, too. My niece, who is four and still calls every dog a doggy, tested this one afternoon by yawning at her grandmother's dog until it yawned back. She now believes that the doggy understands her perfectly. My father, a proud baby boomer, has his own theory: young people yawn more because they stare at screens. Like many boomers, he blames screens for most modern problems.

Last week, in a slow checkout line at the supermarket, I watched a yawn travel from the woman at the register to the man in front of me, then to me, then to the woman behind me. A crowd can carry its own quiet loneliness, and it pleased me that something so small could cross that loneliness in seconds.

I am still a hater of long meetings, but I no longer cringe at the memory of that telecom office. I simply know now that my yawns were never only mine.

Questions:
Why does the columnist still cringe at the memory of one meeting?
Because the manager stopped in the middle of a sentence and asked whether he was keeping the columnist awake.
How does the spreading of yawns follow the lines of intimacy?
We are more likely to catch a yawn from a family member or a close friend than from a stranger.
What does the columnist's niece believe about the doggy?
She believes that the doggy understands her perfectly.
What did the columnist see in the checkout line?
The columnist watched a yawn travel from the woman at the register to the man in front, then to the columnist, then to the woman behind.

lessons.title: Seeing in the Dark
lessons.summary: How the eye slowly adjusts to darkness, and how a young sailor learns to protect her night vision.
lessons.text:
Anyone who has climbed into an attic at night without a light knows the experience. At first the darkness seems complete. After a few minutes, the outlines of boxes and beams begin to appear, and then the shape of an old garden rake leaning against the wall. After half an hour, the attic is surprisingly visible, although every object in it seems to have lost its color.

The first change happens in seconds: the pupil, the black opening at the center of the eye, grows wider. But this accounts for only a small part of the improvement. The real work happens in the thin layer of tissue at the back of the eye, a mosaic of two kinds of light-sensitive cells. Cones work in bright light and allow us to see color. Rods are far more sensitive and take over when the light is dim. In the very center of the mosaic, cones are packed tightly together; toward the edges, rods are the majority.

In daylight, the chemical that allows the rods to respond to light is used up faster than it can be replaced, so they contribute almost nothing. In darkness, the chemical is slowly rebuilt. The cones recover within about ten minutes; then the rods take over, and the eye keeps growing more sensitive for half an hour or more. When this process reaches its climax, the eye is many thousands of times more sensitive than it is at noon. The climax is fragile: a bright light undoes it at once.

Because rods cannot tell colors apart, night vision is monochrome. By moonlight, a red rose looks dark gray, and a garden appears in shades of silver and black, like an old monochrome photograph. Moonlight is many thousands of times weaker than sunlight, yet the rods allow us to cross a field by moonlight without stumbling.

Sailors on night watch depend on these facts. At a vocational school for future ship's officers, a young trainee named Maya learned them during her first winter. Her instructor gave her the autobiography of a retired captain. In his autobiography, the captain explained that he never looked at a lamp before his night watch and that he read his charts by red light, because the rods are hardly affected by red.

On her first night watch, Maya did as the captain had done. When the beam of a passing lighthouse began to rake across the deck, she looked away from it. Slowly, the dark sea revealed its shapes: the line of the shore, a small boat, a single star. The vocational course had taught her the theory; the night taught her the rest. Her instructor said later that she was the calmest trainee he had seen in years.

Questions:
What happens in an attic after half an hour in the dark?
The attic becomes surprisingly visible, although every object seems to have lost its color.
What is the mosaic at the back of the eye made of?
It is a mosaic of two kinds of light-sensitive cells, cones and rods.
Why is night vision monochrome?
Because rods cannot tell colors apart.
What did the captain explain in his autobiography?
He explained that he never looked at a lamp before his night watch and that he read his charts by red light.
What did Maya do when the beam of the lighthouse began to rake across the deck?
She looked away from it.

lessons.title: The Garden in the Gut
lessons.summary: An introduction to the bacteria that live in the human gut and what they do.
lessons.text:
Each of us carries a crowd. In and on the human body live trillions of bacteria, along with smaller numbers of fungi and other tiny organisms, and most of them live in the lower part of the gut. Together they are known as the microbiome. The word has become fashionable in recent years, appearing on yogurt cups, but the science behind it is serious, and it is still young.

An aquarium offers a useful picture. A healthy aquarium is a balanced community: plants, fish and invisible bacteria all depend on one another, and a sudden change in the water can upset the whole tank. The community in the gut is similar. Hundreds of species live there, each with its own needs and its own role, and the conditions around them decide which ones thrive.

Seen up close, however, the gut looks less like a quiet aquarium than a busy hive. As in a hive of bees, the work is divided. Some bacteria break down plant fibers that our own bodies cannot digest, and in doing so they produce substances that feed the cells of the gut wall. Others make vitamins. Still others simply occupy space, leaving little room for harmful visitors to settle. The bacteria also help to train the immune system, teaching it from early childhood which visitors are harmless.

Every meal feeds this community, and different species prefer different foods. A plate of spaghetti with tomato sauce and fresh basil offers a mixture: the spaghetti provides energy, and the tomatoes and the basil offer fiber and other plant substances that certain bacteria favor.

Until recently, a full characterization of these communities was impossible, because most gut bacteria refuse to grow in a laboratory dish. Modern genetic methods have changed that. Researchers can now read the genetic material in a small sample and produce a characterization of nearly every species present, without growing any of them.

The idea reaches beyond human health. Mosquitoes have their own gut bacteria, and researchers studying malaria have found that some of these bacteria make it harder for the malaria parasite to survive inside the insect. Others are studying how the bacteria on human skin shape the smell that draws mosquitoes to some people more than to others.

Many hope that this knowledge will lead to new preventive treatments: rather than fighting a disease after it appears, doctors might one day support the right bacteria before trouble begins. For now, most such preventive ideas remain at the research stage, and many claims printed on fashionable products go far beyond the evidence. The garden in the gut is real, but we are only beginning to learn how to tend it.

Questions:
Why does the text compare the gut to an aquarium?
Because, like a healthy aquarium, it is a balanced community in which many species depend on one another.
How is the gut like a busy hive?
As in a hive of bees, the work is divided among different bacteria.
What does a plate of spaghetti with basil offer the bacteria?
The spaghetti provides energy, and the tomatoes and the basil offer fiber and other plant substances.
Why was a full characterization of these communities impossible until recently?
Because most gut bacteria refuse to grow in a laboratory dish.
What have researchers studying malaria found?
Some bacteria in the mosquito's gut make it harder for the malaria parasite to survive inside the insect.

lessons.title: Fingers in the Pool
lessons.summary: A young swimmer asks why her fingers wrinkle in the water, and her coach explains.
lessons.text:
Every August, during the preseason, the swim team at Lakeside High trained twice a day. Nina was fifteen, the youngest racer on the team, and she spent so many hours in the pool that summer that her fingers seemed permanently wrinkled. One morning, after an hour of practice, she held up her hands and asked her coach, Mr. Alvarez, why water made skin wrinkle.

Mr. Alvarez had studied biology before he became a coach, and he loved questions of this kind. He told her that most people believe the skin simply soaks up water, like a sponge, but that the truth is more interesting. The wrinkles do not appear for about five minutes, and they are controlled by the nerves. When the fingers have been wet for a while, the nerves tell the small blood vessels under the skin to narrow. The tissue beneath the surface shrinks slightly, and the skin above it folds into the familiar pattern. Doctors have noticed that when the nerves in a finger are damaged, that finger does not wrinkle at all.

"So the body does it on purpose?" Nina asked.

Mr. Alvarez said that was the interesting part. Some scientists believe the wrinkles improve our grip on wet objects, the way the grooves in a tire help a car to hold a wet road. In one experiment, people with wrinkled fingers moved wet stones from one box to another faster than people with smooth fingers. Other studies have found smaller effects, so the question is still open.

Nina looked at the long wall of the pool, where a mural showed a school of tuna swimming through blue water. The mural had been painted by students years before, and the swimmers liked it. Mr. Alvarez pointed to it. A tuna, he said, has perfectly smooth skin, because it needs to glide through the water with as little drag as possible. A swimmer wants to glide the same way, which is why racers wear tight caps and smooth suits. Wrinkled fingers, he added with a smile, would not slow her down; her technique mattered far more.

The preseason ended with a qualifier for the state championship. The meet used a knockout format: in each round, only the fastest racers moved on, and the rest were out. Nina swam the 100 meters freestyle. She passed the first knockout round easily and the second by less than a second. In the final of the qualifier, she finished third, which was enough to earn a place at the championship.

As she climbed out of the pool, she looked at her wrinkled fingers and laughed. Then she looked up at the mural, at the smooth, silver tuna, and promised herself that next year she would glide just like them.

Questions:
Why were Nina's fingers wrinkled that summer?
Because she spent many hours in the pool during the preseason.
What causes the skin to wrinkle in water?
The nerves tell the small blood vessels under the skin to narrow, the tissue shrinks slightly, and the skin folds.
What does the mural on the wall show?
It shows a school of tuna swimming through blue water.
Why does a tuna have perfectly smooth skin?
Because it needs to glide through the water with as little drag as possible.
How did the knockout format work at the qualifier?
In each round, only the fastest racers moved on, and the rest were out.

lessons.title: The Town That Wanted Clean Water
lessons.summary: In 1886, a small Canadian town fights for clean drinking water.
lessons.text:
In 1886, the town of Millbrook, in a province of Canada, received its drinking water from a private company. The company took the water from the river just below the town, where the mills and the houses emptied their waste. Every summer, a fever spread through the poorer streets, and every summer the company said that the fever had nothing to do with its water.

The town's doctor, Samuel Reid, did not believe this. He marked each case of fever on a map, and the pattern was clear: the fever appeared almost only in houses that drew water from the company's pipes. Dr. Reid wrote to the company and accused it of negligence. The company replied that it had broken no law, and that negligence could not be proved.

The local newspaper took up the cause. Its columnist, a sharp writer named Agnes Bell, called the river below the mills an atrocity, a word she chose with care. It was an atrocity, she wrote, that children should drink water that no farmer would give to his horses.

The minister of the Presbyterian church, the Reverend Thomas Hale, joined the campaign. Each Sunday, he reminded the Presbyterian families in his church that clean water was not a luxury but an entitlement, something every citizen should receive, rich or poor. The idea of water as an entitlement spread quickly.

Under pressure, the company offered concessions. It promised to build a filter and to lower its prices for the poorest families. The town council considered these concessions and rejected them. It wanted to take over the water supply and move its source above the mills.

The company fought back. Its lawyers argued that a public takeover would be unconstitutional, and that forcing a private business to sell its property was an infringement of the owners' rights. The council's lawyers answered that the province had every right to protect the health of its people, and that the true infringement was on the right of children to drink clean water.

In the end, the matter reached the provincial government. The governing party's caucus met in the capital to discuss a new public health law. Several members of the caucus had doubts, but Dr. Reid's map persuaded most of them. The premier, who had made public health a theme of his premiership, supported the law. It passed in 1887 and allowed towns to build and run their own water systems. Years later, he called it one of the quiet achievements of his premiership.

Two years after that, Millbrook opened a new water plant above the mills. That summer, for the first time anyone could remember, the fever did not return.

Questions:
How did Dr. Reid show that the fever came from the company's water?
He marked each case on a map, and the fever appeared almost only in houses that drew water from the company's pipes.
Why did Agnes Bell call the river an atrocity?
Because children were drinking water that no farmer would give to his horses.
What did the Presbyterian minister tell the families in his church?
He told them that clean water was not a luxury but an entitlement of every citizen, rich or poor.
What concessions did the company offer?
It promised to build a filter and to lower its prices for the poorest families.
What did the company's lawyers argue?
They argued that a public takeover would be unconstitutional and an infringement of the owners' rights.
